974.title: a year of service designed
974.hook: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: Krishna says that's enough
974.carry: a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water
974.howItsDone: In Hindu worship, offerings of flowers, fruit, water and leaves such as tulsi are placed before the deity at home shrines and in temples, and the Gita's verse about a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water is one some devotees recall when making them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a year of service met abhyasa and vairagya: practice that repeats, and a loose hand on the results.

On a temple tray there might be a banana, a few marigolds, a small brass pot of water, a single tulsi leaf. Nothing on it is expensive. Some of it came from a backyard. And the Gita says, in chapter nine, that this is exactly the point. Today, the last piece of our year of service, the one that ties the plan to something larger. It's two verses long, plain enough to say over a lunch tray.
screen: `A BANANA, MARIGOLDS, WATER, A LEAF.` → `NOTHING EXPENSIVE.` → `THE LAST PIECE OF THE PLAN.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in paraphrase: whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from a striving heart, I accept. Things anyone can find. The verse doesn't rank them or ask for more. What it asks for is bhakti, devotion, the love behind the hand that holds it out. Then the next verse widens the tray to hold the whole day. Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give, whatever discipline you take on, do it as an offering to me. Read with this week in mind, the verse changes what a year of service is. Up to now, the design has been about the work: the good of all beings, svadharma, the gift, the guest, the rhythm. This verse says the work itself can be laid on the tray. The meal for a guest is an offering. The gift given without expecting return is an offering. A Tuesday shift almost skipped is an offering. Even the eating, the verse says, and that's ordinary on purpose. Some Hindus speak of this verse as the place where service and worship meet, so that seva in a temple and puja at a home shrine are one act in two places. Across Hindu homes and temples, the same small offerings go before Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess and others. The shape stays: small things, given with love, count. And that's where tomorrow begins: bhakti, and a love poem about Krishna and Radha.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, MAKE IT AN OFFERING.` · `THE WORK GOES ON THE TRAY.` · `SMALL THINGS, GIVEN WITH LOVE, COUNT.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE YEAR AS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: If there's a small thing within reach, a leaf, a glass of water, a piece of fruit, hold it in your hands; if not, just open them. Let the year you've sketched come to mind piece by piece, the reason, your own service, the gift, the guest, the rhythm, and set each one on the tray in your hands until it feels full. If you pray, you can offer it to the one you pray to; if not, just rest with the weight of it.
Puja. Worship, the offering of a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, and whatever you do, eat, give or practice, laid down as small as a leaf.
Your line: a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water. Small things, given with love. See you tomorrow.

975.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
975.hook: the sky is dark with clouds, and Radha is told to take him home
975.howItsDone: Songs from the Gita Govinda are sung in Hindu devotional settings and performed in classical music and dance, and the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare is sung on its own as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, puja: a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water, and the whole year of service laid on the tray as an offering.
screen: `A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.`

segments.voice: The sky is heavy with clouds. The forest is dark with tamala trees. Night is coming on, and the boy is nervous. So Nanda, the cowherd chief, turns to Radha: take him home. That's how the Gita Govinda begins, with a walk home through the dark. And the verse hails what follows on the bank of the river Yamuna: the secret love of Radha and Madhava, one of Krishna's names. After our days on the Bhagavad Gita, the path turns from Krishna the teacher on a battlefield to Krishna the beloved in a forest.
screen: `CLOUDS, DARK TREES, NIGHT.` → `TAKE HIM HOME.` → `FROM BATTLEFIELD TO FOREST.`

segments.voice: Gita Govinda means the song of Govinda, the cowherd, another name for Krishna. It's a love poem, and it says so up front. A few lines in, Jayadeva gives an invitation. If your heart is moved by remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to these sweet, soft, lovely words of Jayadeva. Both conditions in one sentence: remembering God and the play of lovers, offered as a single door. That pairing is the heart of what the poem means by bhakti. The word means devotion, loving attention, and in the Gita we just finished, Krishna praised it as a way to him. Here bhakti stops being a teaching and becomes a song. Before the love story starts, though, Jayadeva sings a hymn through the Lord's descents into the world, the avatars: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and on through Rama and the Buddha to Kalki, one stanza each. Every stanza ends with the same refrain: jaya jagadisha hare, victory to you, Hari, Lord of the world. So the reader meets the cosmic Lord first, the one who saves worlds in many forms, and only then the timid boy Radha is walking home under the clouds. The poem holds both at once. In the stories to come, Radha's longing for Krishna, and his for her, are read by some devotees as the soul's longing for God and God's for the soul. Jayadeva doesn't explain that; he just sings.
screen: `THE SONG OF GOVINDA, THE COWHERD.` · `REMEMBERING HARI, AND THE ARTS OF LOVE.` · `A HYMN TO THE LORD'S DESCENTS.` · `THE COSMIC LORD, THEN THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `JAYA JAGADISHA HARE.`

segments.voice: Hear the opening again, clouds, dark trees, night coming, someone asked to walk another home, and let your mind find a person you've walked home in some way: driven, waited with, stayed on the phone with until they were safe. Breathe with that memory. If you pray, you can let the refrain move quietly with the breath, jaya jagadisha hare; if not, just stay with the picture of two figures walking under the clouds.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda, it's sung: remembering Hari and the play of love, through one door.
Your line: take him home. Tomorrow, spring, and Radha at the edge of the dance. That's day nine hundred seventy-five.

976.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
976.hook: spring arrives in the forest, and Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone but her
976.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotion, the Gita Govinda's songs of Radha's longing are sung and danced, and viraha, longing in separation, is honored as a mood of devotion in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the opening of the Gita Govinda: dark clouds, Radha told to take him home, and the refrain jaya jagadisha hare.

Clove vines curl in a soft southern breeze. Bees hum around the flowering trees. The cuckoo is calling. Jayadeva piles up the details of spring until the forest seems almost too sweet to stand in. Into it walks Radha, with a friend at her side, and the friend points. Look. There's Hari, playing in the spring woods, dancing with the young cowherd women. The song's refrain says this season is hard on anyone apart from the one they love. And Radha is standing at the edge of the dance, apart.
screen: `CLOVE VINES, BEES, THE CUCKOO.` → `LOOK: HARI IS DANCING.` → `RADHA, AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The friend keeps singing, in paraphrase. Here, in the lovely spring, Hari plays, dancing with the young women: a cruel season for those apart from love. She describes him, one woman after another drawing close, each sure she has his attention. And Radha, the poem says, goes away. Not to confront him. She slips off into a bower of vines, hurt and jealous, and sits by herself. She doesn't stop loving him. In her song, she remembers him: the flute, the playful glances, the way he looked at her. Even while she's angry, her mind keeps returning to Hari. She tells her friend that her heart won't let him go, though he's with the others. That's the bhakti the poem cares about. Devotion, in the Gita Govinda, isn't calm. It isn't a pleasant feeling on a good day. It has jealousy in it, and hurt, and memory, and the stubborn turning of the heart back to the one it loves. Some Vaishnava traditions have a name for this longing in separation, viraha, and treat it as a doorway rather than a failure. Radha's ache at the edge of the dance becomes, for them, a picture of the soul when God seems to be everywhere except close. The poem doesn't scold her for being jealous, and doesn't hurry to fix things. It lets her sit in the bower and remember. Spring keeps blooming around her the whole time. And somewhere in the forest, as we'll hear tomorrow, Krishna has noticed she's gone.
screen: `HARI DANCES IN THE SPRING WOODS.` · `RADHA SLIPS AWAY TO A BOWER.` · `SHE KEEPS REMEMBERING HIM.` · `VIRAHA: LONGING IN SEPARATION.` · then, large: `THE HEART TURNS BACK.`

If you pray, you can bring that longing, as it is, to the one you pray to; if not, let spring keep blooming around the feeling.

977.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
977.hook: Krishna sits alone by the Yamuna, and the god of the poem admits he let her walk away
977.carry: God is the one who misses
977.howItsDone: Singers in Vaishnava communities perform the Gita Govinda's songs in temples and in concert, often one song at a time, and dancers in classical forms such as Odissi act out scenes like Krishna's lament by the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and Radha slipping away from the spring dance into a bower of vines, still remembering him.

Krishna is sitting by the river Yamuna, alone, and he is not doing well. A little while ago he was at the center of a spring dance in the forest, everyone around him. Then he noticed someone missing. Radha had seen him there, surrounded, and had quietly gone. He left the dance and searched the thickets and the vine bowers. Nothing. Now he has sat down on the bank, and Jayadeva lets us listen while he talks to himself. It isn't the speech a listener might expect from a god.
screen: `A DANCE, AND SOMEONE MISSING.` → `HE SEARCHES THE THICKETS.` → `ALONE ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: Here is his song, in paraphrase. She saw me surrounded by the other women, and she walked away. I didn't stop her. I was afraid, because I knew I was in the wrong. Then the refrain, again and again: Hari, Hari, through my own carelessness she has gone, angry, it seems. What will she do now? What will she say to me, after I've been away so long? What good is wealth, or people, or a home, without her? He sees her face in his mind, the eyebrows drawn together in anger, and speaks to her as if she were there: forgive me, I won't do it again, let me see you. This is the Lord of the poem, the one the opening hymn praised in every one of his descents into the world. And here he sits, admitting a mistake. How do devotees hold this? In Vaishnava traditions, one answer is the word lila, play. The divine takes on a lover's part fully, faults and all, so that love can be shown in its whole range: delight, hurt, regret, longing. It's easy to picture bhakti running one way, the soul reaching up toward God. Here it runs the other way too. God is the one who misses, rehearsing an apology by the river. And Jayadeva closes his songs by naming himself, offering what he has sung. So even in Krishna's lament there's a third voice in the room, quietly saying: I made this as an offering.

If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply stay with the memory, and breathe.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda it runs both ways: today, the one who longs is Krishna.

978.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
978.hook: sandal paste and moonlight are supposed to cool you down, and in Radha's bower they burn
978.howItsDone: In Vaishnava kirtan and in classical dance, the Gita Govinda is performed song by song, and the friend's report of Radha's state, with its refrain on her separation, is one of the songs performers take up.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti ran the other way: Krishna alone by the Yamuna, admitting he let Radha walk away. God is the one who misses.

Sandal paste on the skin. Moonlight through the leaves. A soft wind off the southern hills. In poems like this one, these are the comforts of a hot evening, the things that cool a body down. Now a friend of Radha's comes to Krishna, where he waits in the forest, with a report. Everything that ought to soothe her, she says, is burning her. This is Radha's side, carried by someone who has just been sitting with her.
screen: `SANDAL, MOONLIGHT, A SOFT WIND.` → `A FRIEND COMES WITH A REPORT.` → `RADHA'S SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the friend's song, in paraphrase. She blames the sandal paste. She blames the rays of the moon. They don't cool her; they torment her. The breeze from the sandalwood hills feels to her like poison. She lies on a bed of leaves and flowers and gets no rest. And the refrain keeps returning: in separation from you, Krishna, she is miserable. Two days ago we met the word for this ache, viraha. Today the poem shows what it does to the world around her. The comforts haven't changed. The moon is the same moon. But the one she loves isn't there, so every sweet thing turns into a reminder of what's missing. Ordinary grief knows a small version: a song comes on in a shop, a smell drifts from a kitchen, and something pleasant becomes hard to bear. Here the poem becomes devotion, not only love poetry. Some Vaishnava readers hear Radha as the soul and Krishna as God. In Chaitanya's tradition, Radha is Krishna's own power of love, and the soul stands nearer her friends, watching. Read either way, nothing in the world has gone wrong. Her attention has gone entirely to one place, and everything else points there. And notice who carries it. The friend doesn't argue Radha out of her grief, and she doesn't scold Krishna. She sits with one, walks to the other, and tells the truth about what she saw. In the Gita Govinda, even the go-between's report is a song.
screen: `THE MOON AND SANDAL BURN HER.` · `THE SAME MOON, WITHOUT HIM.` · `EVERY SWEET THING A REMINDER.` · `THE FRIEND TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `IN SEPARATION FROM YOU, SHE IS MISERABLE.`

segments.voice: Feel the cool air at the edge of the nostrils for a few breaths, then let one small comfort around you come into focus: the chair holding you, a cup nearby, the light in the room. Let it lead you to someone who isn't here to share it, far away or gone, and let the comfort and the missing sit side by side. If you pray, offer that longing as your prayer; if you don't, let the breath keep coming, cool, and let the person stay in mind.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the friend's report, it's attention so full that even the cooling moon points back to the one who isn't there.
Your line: the same moon, without him. Nothing changed but who was missing. Day nine hundred seventy-eight, done.

979.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
979.hook: Radha waits all night in the place they agreed on, and at dawn he finally turns up
979.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional performance, Radha's mana, her loving anger, is a recognized mood: singers and Odissi or Bharatanatyam dancers perform her song of dismissal at dawn as part of the Gita Govinda's story of separation and reunion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti in the friend's report, moonlight and sandal paste burning Radha. The same moon, without him.

The plan was simple: meet in the bower by the river, tonight. Radha goes. She waits. The moon comes up over the forest, and he doesn't come. She hears a leaf move and thinks it's him. It isn't. The whole night goes by like that. Then, at dawn, there he is, walking up through the trees with the look of someone who hasn't slept. Before he can say a word, she knows where he's been. What does a devotee, in a poem about God, say to God at a moment like this? Jayadeva gives her the floor.
screen: `MEET IN THE BOWER TONIGHT.` → `THE MOON RISES. NO ONE.` → `AT DAWN, THERE HE IS.`

segments.voice: The poem lingers on what she sees, in paraphrase. His eyes are red from a night without sleep. There are marks on him, traces left by someone else. And her song has a refrain sharp enough to sting: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Don't speak your deceiving words. Go to the one who kept you up all night. She doesn't soften it or pretend to be fine. And the poem doesn't correct her, not yet. It lets her anger stand on the page, in front of the one the poem calls Lord. Vaishnava poetics has a name for this loving anger: mana, the wounded pride of a lover who knows her worth. It's treated as one of love's real moods, not a fault to hide. Read, as some devotees read it, with Radha as the soul, the scene suggests that bhakti doesn't have to be polite. A devotee may come before God disappointed, even furious, and the relationship holds. In the poem it more than holds: Krishna won't stop seeking her. Later, her friend will gently tell her she's held on long enough. But first, the poem gives her this. An honest complaint is itself a way of staying in the room. Indifference would say nothing. Radha says everything. And Jayadeva, who signs the song as his offering, lets her.
screen: `RED EYES. MARKS. NO SLEEP.` · `GO, MADHAVA. GO, KESHAVA.` · `MANA: LOVE'S WOUNDED PRIDE.` · `THE COMPLAINT KEEPS HER IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `DON'T SPEAK YOUR DECEIVING WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop and bring to mind one disappointment you've been carrying quietly, with a person, with life, or with God, if God is part of your life. Don't argue it away or make it bigger; just name it to yourself, plainly, the way Radha does, and notice that you're still here, still facing it. If you pray, bring it into your prayer just as it is; if you don't, let it be said inside, and keep breathing.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the Gita Govinda it has room for mana, love's honest anger, which still keeps facing the beloved.
Your line: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Even her go-away kept her facing him. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine.

980.title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
980.hook: every scene this week has someone remembering someone, and the poet named that before the story began
980.carry: let the beloved come back to mind
980.howItsDone: In bhakti traditions, smarana, remembering the deity, is practiced through repeating a divine name, singing, and hearing stories; Vaishnava devotees sing the Gita Govinda's songs as one way of keeping Krishna in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti with an edge. Radha at dawn, go, Madhava, go, Keshava, and love's honest anger.

Krishna, alone by the river, keeps seeing Radha's face. Radha, in her bower, can't look at the moon without thinking of him. At dawn, every sharp word she says is about him. Run back through these scenes from the Gita Govinda and one thing keeps happening: somebody is remembering somebody. Jayadeva put a name to it before the story began, in an opening verse we heard on the first day. He gave remembering Hari as a reason to listen at all. On our last day with Jayadeva, that one word gets a closer look.
screen: `SOMEONE REMEMBERING SOMEONE.` → `THE POET NAMED IT FIRST.` → `TODAY: ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse once more, in paraphrase. If your heart is drawn to remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to Jayadeva's words: sweet, soft and lovely. On the first day, the point was the double invitation. Today, the first of the two. Remembering is smarana, and in the Bhagavata it names a practice. The boy Prahlada lists the ways of devotion there, and among them are hearing about Vishnu, singing about him, and remembering him. In that company, remembering isn't something that simply happens. It's something done: letting the beloved come back to mind, again and again, in the middle of ordinary life. And the poem is full of it. Krishna sees Radha's brows drawn together in anger. Radha finds even the moon a reminder. At dawn, her anger is all about him. Nobody in this poem is calm, and nobody forgets. The story doesn't leave them apart: her friend coaxes her, Krishna comes back and pleads, and Radha goes to him. The opening verse names what the poem offers a listener: a way of filling the mind with the beloved. Just before the Gita Govinda, we sketched a year of service, the work of the hands, and the Gita's verse about a leaf, a flower and some water laid all of it on one tray. Smarana is an offering that needs no tray. The hands can be still while the mind brings the beloved back.
screen: `THE FIRST IF: REMEMBERING HARI.` · `PRAHLADA'S LIST: HEAR, SING, REMEMBER.` · `NOBODY IN THE POEM FORGETS.` · `AN OFFERING THAT NEEDS NO TRAY.` · then, large: `SMARANA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, or, if you pray, the form of God you pray to, and let their face come back. When the mind drifts, notice where it went and bring the face back, gently; that return is the practice. If you pray, let a name you already use rest in the mind; if you don't, let the face be enough.
Bhakti. Devotion. This week the Gita Govinda showed it as longing on both sides, honest anger, and smarana, remembering the beloved again and again.
Your line: let the beloved come back to mind. That's the last of our Gita Govinda days. Until tomorrow.
